findings.title: OAuth `state` is the static pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce
findings.body:
The OAuth `state` sent to GitHub, and later checked at line 412, is `pipeline.signature`. That value is an md5 of the pipeline view class names, so it is identical for every user, session and installation. The tests confirm this by hardcoding "9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3".

Because it is constant and publicly derivable, the `state` check gives no CSRF or login-CSRF protection. An attacker can build a valid callback URL with their own `code` and the known state. The victim's pipeline would then bind the attacker's GitHub identity as `github_authenticated_user`.

The existing `OAuth2LoginView` already does this correctly: it generates `secrets.token_hex()`, binds it with `pipeline.bind_state("state", ...)`, and compares the callback against the stored value. The same should be done here. As written, the PR description's claim that a `state` mismatch is detected is not meaningfully true.

findings.title: User verification is bypassed when the Integration row does not yet exist
findings.body:
The check that the authenticated GitHub user matches the installer only runs on the branch where the Integration exists and has no OrganizationIntegration. When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises DoesNotExist, the view returns `pipeline.next_step()` with no check. `build_integration` then creates the integration from the attacker-supplied `installation_id`.

This happens whenever the `installation` webhook has not arrived yet, is delayed, or failed. In those cases anyone who supplies another account's installation_id (these are sequential integers) can still link that GitHub installation to their own Sentry org.

The fix is to validate the installer independently of the local DB row, for example by fetching the installation sender from GitHub or by rejecting the request. Otherwise the protection this PR describes is incomplete.

findings.title: KeyError (500) when existing Integration metadata has no `sender`
findings.body:
`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every Integration was created by the installation webhook. `build_integration` only adds `sender` when it is present in state, and the pipeline path never puts it there. Integrations created through the pipeline (see `test_basic_flow`'s expected metadata, which has no `sender`) or older ones therefore lack this key.

If such an org removes the Sentry-side installation, leaving the Integration in place without an OrganizationIntegration, and later reinstalls, this line raises KeyError. The user gets an unhandled 500 instead of either a successful install or the error page. Use `.get()` and decide on explicit handling for a missing sender.

findings.title: Network/HTTP failures in the OAuth exchange are not handled and surface as 500s
findings.body:
Two calls in the OAuth exchange are not handled:

- `get_user_info()` calls `raise_for_status()`, so a non-2xx from GitHub's `/user` endpoint (revoked token, rate limit, outage) raises `requests.HTTPError`.
- `safe_urlopen` at line 423 sits outside the try block and can raise on connection errors or timeouts.

Neither is caught. Instead of the intended `github-integration-failed.html` page with `postMessage` back to the opener, the user gets a server error and the setup dialog breaks. Wrap both calls and return `error(...)` on failure.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path
findings.body:
The test now sends a `state` value ("ddd023d8...") that does not match the pipeline signature. The OAuth view therefore rejects the request with "Invalid installation request." before the GitHub 404 for `/app/installations/{id}` is ever reached.

The previous assertion on "The GitHub installation could not be found.", i.e. the `IntegrationError` raised in `build_integration` on a 404, is gone. That path no longer has coverage, and the test name is now misleading. Use the valid state, finish the flow, and assert the 404 message; add a separate test for the state mismatch.

findings.title: No test for the success path where the webhook-created sender matches the authenticated user
findings.body:
`test_github_user_mismatch` covers only the rejection case. No test covers an Integration created by the webhook, with no OrganizationIntegration, whose `sender.login` equals the OAuth-authenticated user and so completes successfully. That is the main path the new check affects.

The existing success tests all go through the `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch, so a regression that blocks legitimate installs on the sender-match branch would not be caught.
